query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a dense, adherent TiB2 ceramic coating to the metal parts of hot dip aluminum plating equipment will reduce the chemical erosion caused by high-temperature liquid aluminum, thereby extending the service life of these components.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional metal substrates (e.g., steel or similar alloys) used in components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates that are prone to rapid corrosion when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Deposit a dense, non-wetting TiB2 ceramic layer on the surface of the metal parts using physical vapor deposition or plasma spraying.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, long-term exposure to molten aluminum during the plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The TiB2 coating forms a chemically inert, continuous barrier with low wettability, effectively isolating the metal substrate from direct contact with the liquid aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The inert and thermally stable TiB2 layer minimizes the chemical interaction and penetration of aluminum, reducing corrosion and erosion by limiting the wetting and reactive contact between molten aluminum and the underlying metal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated components will exhibit significantly reduced erosion and chemical attack from the molten aluminum, leading to a noticeably extended service life compared to uncoated parts.
generation.baseline: Erosion rate and service life of conventional metal parts without a protective coating when exposed to high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is contingent on the coating remaining dense, adherent, and intact under operational thermal and mechanical stresses. Degradation or failure of the coating due to defects or extreme conditions may diminish its effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of service life improvement and erosion reduction remains uncertain and is likely dependent on the applied coating’s quality, thickness, and adhesion. Further optimization and testing are required to quantify improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of test coupons with identical metal substrate: one set coated with a dense TiB2 layer (via physical vapor deposition or plasma spraying) and one set left uncoated. Subject both sets to laboratory-simulated hot dip aluminum plating conditions with controlled temperature, immersion time, and mechanical stresses representative of real-world operation.
measurements: Quantitative weight loss measurements to assess erosion rates over time
Surface analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS) to evaluate coating integrity and extent of corrosion
Adhesion tests to ensure the coating remains stable under thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiB2-coated coupons do not show a statistically significant reduction in erosion or an extension of useful service life compared to the uncoated coupons under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ]. decision.trend: Earlier work in high‐temperature materials has largely focused on designing bulk alloys – especially high entropy and refractory high‐entropy systems – by modifying their compositions and processing routes to enhance phase stability, secondary phase formation (e.g., in situ Al2O3 or ceramic reinforcements), and overall mechanical performance at elevated temperatures. These studies evolved from conventional metal processing toward using complex alloying (with additions such as Ti, Mo, Hf) and advanced synthesis techniques (e.g., spark plasma sintering, sputtering) to improve strength and oxidation resistance. However, while such composition and processing changes improved high‐temperature strength and, in some cases, oxidation behavior, none addressed the unique challenge of long-term chemical or erosive attack from a corrosive molten metal environment such as high‐temperature liquid aluminum.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge remains how to protect equipment components from the aggressive chemical attack and erosion incurred during extended contact with hot, liquid aluminum. Bulk alloy modifications alone do not provide a dedicated chemical barrier at the interface with molten aluminum, so the issue of interfacial compatibility and chemical inertness remains unsolved.
decision.lever: Apply a dense, adherent ceramic protective coating – for example, a TiB2 (or similarly inert ceramic) layer deposited via physical vapor deposition or plasma spraying – tailored for low wettability and high chemical stability with molten aluminum.
decision.why: This step follows naturally from the trend where bulk composition changes have been used to achieve high-temperature strength and stability but have not directly addressed contact corrosion. A surface engineering solution that creates a chemically inert barrier specifically at the interface will directly counter the root cause (long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum) and is the most plausible next move given the design gap and process cues.
